lede: A hand warmer gets hot, a cold pack gets cold, and both are reactions. The difference is only which way the heat travels — and at Higher you can work out which it will be before you mix anything.
can: Tell exothermic from endothermic by what the thermometer does.
Draw and label a reaction profile with its activation energy and energy change.
Calculate an energy change from bond energies and read its sign.

md: A hand warmer gets hot; a cold pack gets cold. Both are chemical reactions, and the difference between them is simply which way the heat goes. This topic gives you the two words, the picture and, at Higher, the arithmetic that predicts which one you will get.

prompt: In the cup shown, the temperature went from 21.0 °C to 27.5 °C. What was the temperature rise, in °C?
explain: 27.5 − 21.0 = 6.5 °C. Finish minus start, in that order, or the sign comes out backwards.

text: 1. Two words, and how to tell them apart

md: A reaction that **gives out heat** is **exothermic**: the mixture and its surroundings get **hotter**, so the thermometer reading **rises**. A reaction that **takes heat in** is **endothermic**: the mixture gets **colder** and the reading **falls**. Burning, neutralisation and most metal-and-acid reactions are exothermic; thermal decomposition and a cold pack dissolving are endothermic.

title: Why the thermometer is the evidence and the word is not
md: What you can measure is the temperature going up or down. *Exothermic* is the conclusion you draw from that measurement. An examiner asking for an observation wants the measurement; an examiner asking for the type of reaction wants the word.

prompt: In the cup experiment shown above, the temperature rose by 6.5 °C. What kind of reaction is it?
explain: Exothermic: the temperature went up, so heat was given out to the surroundings.

alt: An energy-against-progress graph for an exothermic reaction: the reactant level, a hump, and a lower product level, with the height of the hump marked as the activation energy and the drop between the levels marked as the energy change.
svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 700 400" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img" aria-labelledby="cpr"><title id="cpr">An exothermic reaction profile: energy against progress of reaction, with a hump between the reactant level and the product level</title><g fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.6"><path d="M70 330 H660"/><path d="M70 330 V80"/></g><path d="M96 150 H192 C246 150 252 72 368 72 C484 72 490 268 544 268 H640" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2.2"/><g fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.1" stroke-dasharray="4 4"><path d="M96 150 H498"/><path d="M640 268 H498"/></g><g fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.3"><path d="M278 150 V78"/><path d="M274 84 l4 -6 l4 6"/><path d="M488 150 V268"/><path d="M484 262 l4 6 l4 -6"/></g><g font-family="inherit" font-size="12" fill="currentColor"><text x="168" y="106">activation energy</text><text x="480" y="213" text-anchor="end">energy change</text></g><g font-family="inherit" font-size="12.5" fill="currentColor"><text x="76" y="140">reactants</text><text x="574" y="258">products</text><text x="368" y="368" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="500">Progress of reaction</text><text transform="translate(40 210) rotate(-90)" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="500">Energy</text><text x="70" y="52" font-size="13" font-weight="600">Reaction profile</text></g></svg>
caption: Exothermic: the products sit lower than the reactants, so energy has been given out.

md: A **reaction profile** puts energy up the page and the progress of the reaction across it. The **reactants** start at one level and the **products** finish at another. In an **exothermic** reaction the products are **lower**, and the drop between the levels is the **energy change**. The hump between them is the **activation energy**: the **minimum energy needed for a reaction to occur**.

prompt: On the reaction profile above, where do the products sit compared with the reactants, and what does that tell you?
options: lower, so the reaction is exothermic
higher, so the reaction is exothermic
lower, so the reaction is endothermic
answer: lower, so the reaction is exothermic
explain: Lower products means energy has left the chemicals, so it is exothermic. Endothermic profiles finish higher than they start.

text: 3. Drawing one that earns the marks

alt: An energy-against-progress graph for an endothermic reaction: the product level sits above the reactant level, and the hump is higher than both.
svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 700 400" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img" aria-labelledby="cpr"><title id="cpr">An endothermic reaction profile: energy against progress of reaction, with a hump between the reactant level and the product level</title><g fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.6"><path d="M70 330 H660"/><path d="M70 330 V80"/></g><path d="M96 268 H192 C246 268 252 72 368 72 C484 72 490 150 544 150 H640" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2.2"/><g fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.1" stroke-dasharray="4 4"><path d="M96 268 H498"/><path d="M640 150 H498"/></g><g fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.3"><path d="M278 268 V78"/><path d="M274 84 l4 -6 l4 6"/><path d="M488 268 V150"/><path d="M484 156 l4 -6 l4 6"/></g><g font-family="inherit" font-size="12" fill="currentColor"><text x="168" y="106">activation energy</text><text x="480" y="213" text-anchor="end">energy change</text></g><g font-family="inherit" font-size="12.5" fill="currentColor"><text x="76" y="258">reactants</text><text x="574" y="140">products</text><text x="368" y="368" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="500">Progress of reaction</text><text transform="translate(40 210) rotate(-90)" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="500">Energy</text><text x="70" y="52" font-size="13" font-weight="600">Reaction profile</text></g></svg>
caption: Endothermic: the same shape, but the products finish above the reactants.

md: Four marks, four separate things. **One** smooth reaction-pathway line, not two. The **product level** on the correct side — below for exothermic, above for endothermic. The **activation energy** arrow drawn from the **reactant** level up to the **top of the hump**. The **energy change** arrow drawn between the two **levels**. Use single-headed arrows, and keep the whole curve above the horizontal axis.

title: What the 2024 report asked for
md: Candidates were told to use **only single-headed arrows** on these diagrams, to keep the **product line above the x-axis**, and to draw **only one line** for the reaction pathway. Those three instructions are the difference between four marks and two.

prompt: On a reaction profile, where does the activation energy arrow start and end?
options: at the reactant level, ending at the top of the hump
at the product level, ending at the top of the hump
at the reactant level, ending at the product level
answer: at the reactant level, ending at the top of the hump
explain: It measures the climb the reactants must make. The arrow between the two levels is the energy change, which is the other label.

caption: Break first, make second: energy in, then energy out.

md:
**Breaking** a bond **takes energy in**; **making** a bond **gives energy out**. So:
**energy change = energy taken in to break bonds − energy given out when bonds are made**.
**The question.** $\ce{H2 + Cl2 -> 2HCl}$, with H–H 436, Cl–Cl 242 and H–Cl 431 kJ.
**Step 1 — bonds broken.** One H–H and one Cl–Cl: 436 + 242 = 678 kJ.

prompt: Step 2. Two molecules of HCl form, each with one H–Cl bond worth 431 kJ. How much energy, in kJ, is given out making those bonds?
explain: 2 × 431 = 862 kJ. Count the bonds in every molecule, not once for each kind: 431 on its own is the commonest wrong route here.

md:
**Step 3 — subtract, in the right order.** 678 − 862 = -184 kJ.
**Step 4 — read the sign.** It is **negative**, so more energy came out than went in: the reaction is **exothermic**. A negative answer is the sign that the reaction gives out heat, and Summer 2023's report records candidates losing the mark by leaving it off.

prompt: The energy change for that reaction came out as -184 kJ. What does the sign tell you?
options: more energy was given out than taken in, so it is exothermic
more energy was taken in than given out, so it is endothermic
the two are equal, so there is no energy change
answer: more energy was given out than taken in, so it is exothermic
explain: Negative means exothermic. Keep the minus sign on the answer line: it is part of the answer, not decoration.

text: 5. The same reaction the other way

md: Run that reaction backwards — $\ce{2HCl -> H2 + Cl2}$ — and every bond that was made must now be broken, and every bond that was broken must now be made. The arithmetic simply swaps over: 862 − 678 = +184 kJ. **Same size, opposite sign**, so the reverse reaction is **endothermic**. If your two answers do not mirror each other like that, one of them has a slip in it.

title: GCSE Chemistry - Bond Energies - Determining if Reactions are Exothermic or Endothermic
why: A second worked calculation, with the subtraction set out the same way round.

prompt: The forward reaction has an energy change of -184 kJ. What is the energy change, in kJ, for the reverse reaction?
explain: +184 kJ. The same bonds are involved, so the size cannot change; only the direction, and therefore the sign, does.

md:
say that **exothermic** means heat given out and the temperature rises, and **endothermic** the opposite.
draw a reaction profile with one pathway line, the product level on the right side, and both arrows labelled.
define **activation energy** as the minimum energy needed for a reaction to occur.
recall that **breaking** bonds **takes energy in** and **making** bonds **gives energy out**.
calculate **bonds broken − bonds made**, count every bond in every molecule, and read the sign.

This is Question 6 of the Higher C2 paper. The first mark is usually the product level on the right side of the profile; the last is the sign on the energy change. Stuck in a calculation? Write bonds broken and bonds made as two separate totals before you subtract. The Sheet below lists the traps.
